PUISNE JUDGE REVISES
DECISION.

label: paragraph_title
text: ON A RENTS CASE

label: text
text: On the grounds that he "went astray" on a certain point, Mr. Justice Wood," in the Summary Court this morning, revised a judgment given on a claim by a landlord against Mr. Albert Guefat, proprietor of Cafe Albert, in respect of rent for his residence.

label: text
text: In a previous judgment His Honour found for defendants on claim and counterclaim (defendant alleged that he had paid the rent as well as had certain fitness put in the house for which the landlord was lable).

label: text
text: This morning, His Honour said that, with the help of the able argument submitted by Mr. M. K. Lo, an error in his original judgment had been shown. He had given judgment for the tenant on the landlord's claim for rent on the supposition that his defence to the claim was "release" in respect of it.

label: text
text: This defence had been supported by the evidence furnished for the landlord. "It seemed to me," said His Honour, "that the landlord was estopped by his agent's conduct from denying the'release.' "I gave judgment for the tenant, as I now think, on insufficient consideration.

label: text
text: "The distinction between'release', and 'payment' had been kept clearly before my mind. If the plea of'release' was to be relied upon, it was necessary" to prove that something, less than full payment was expected in satisfaction of the claim.

label: text
text: "On the other hand, a plan of 'payment' necessitated proof of payment of the child in full. This is a case where pleadings would have been of service in defining the real issues." "Release" was, in fact, never a part of the tenant's own case. It was suggested solely from the evidence of the landlord's agent. The tenant's case was "payment" not "release."

label: text
text: "I went astray," continued His Honour, "in assuming that it was material to find whether the Oxford's receipt was issued for cash or for some other consideration." "The question is material for the reason that the issue raised by the tenant's defence was 'payment' and nothing else, cash payment or no cash payment."

label: text
text: "On this issue, again, the landlord's case is not hampered by estoppel." The receipt given is a final discharge for the claim for rent, for the rent was paid in full and not otherwise. The landlord, having given the receipt to the tenant, is not thereby estopped from claiming a payment of rent from him, for the rent has not been, in fact, paid. The orus of proving payment is thereby on the tenant.

label: text
text: “As I have previously explained, I have not been satisfied that payment has been either proved or disproved by the evidence in the case. On these grounds, I now consider that judgment should be given for the landlord on the claim. The judgment on the counterclaim is reaffirmed each party to pay their own costs.”

label: paragraph_title
text: VINEGAR CASE

label: paragraph_title
text: SUMMONS AGAINST CHINESE DEALER.

label: text
text: PROSECUTION FAILS.

label: text
text: An interesting point arose in the prosecution brought by the Sanitary Department, against a Shauki-wan shopkeeper for selling vinegar which did not approach the universal standard of 4 per cent. acetic acid content.

label: text
text:
Both Mr. E. R. Dovey, the Government Analyst, and Dr. A. G. M. Severn (Assistint M.O.H.) were present this morning to hear the decision of Mr. R. E. Lindsell since the adjournment made last week to enable him to look up old cases.
Questioned by the Magistrate,
Signatory Inspector Gregory said he
was unaware that there were two

label: text
text: Mr. Lindsell said he was satisfied that there were two sorts of vinegar sold. If a customer went to a shop and asked for "Cho" he would get Chinese vinegar, and if he asked for foreign vinegar he was entitled to get vinegar with 4 percent acetic acid. In the present case Chinese vinegar was asked for and this was supplied. No offence had therefore been committed.

label: text
text: Dr. Severn pointed out that the defendant supplies the Chinese shops with this vinegar and, they sell it in bottles.

label: text
text: His Worship held there was no proof of this, and said the proper remedy was to proceed against the shops selling Chinese vinegar in bottles with the word "vinegar" printed in English.

label: text
text: The summons was dismissed.

label: paragraph_title
text: WEST POINT FIRE

label: text
text: MEDICINE SHOF ABLAZE AT MIDNIGHT.

label: text
text: $2,500 DAMAGE.

label: text
text: At 12:45 this morning the Central Fire Station received a call to deal with a fire which had broken out at No.438, Queen's Road West, ground floor, used as a Chinese medicine shop.

label: text
text:
Apolliances from Kennedy Town and Central Station arrived simultaneously on the scene, followed by the Wanchai equipment on a "home call" sent five minutes later.
On the arrival of the Brigade, the contents of the floor, which comprised in addition to herbs a large quantity of bottled drugs, were well alight. With two deliveries working from the front and rear of the shop, the fire was extinguished in ten minutes.

label: header
text: THE CHINA MAIL.

label: text
text: Although the greater part of the stock was destroyed or otherwise damaged by water, the timely arrival of the Brigade and their quick work saved some portions of the fittings and confined the fire to the ground floor. There being no staircase inside the building, the fire did not spread to the two upper floors, which were practically untouched.

label: text
text:
On "investigations · being made the fire was found to have started from burning joys" sticks placed under wooden shelves. These contained carboard boxes which quickly came within the range of the fire and in turn set alight the dry stocks of medicine leaves.
The contents of the medicine shop were insured for $1,100 jointly between the Heung On Insurance Company and the Sincere Company.
Including stock, fittings and fire damage to the ground floor of the building, the total loss is estimated at about $2,500.

text: NO POWER?

label: paragraph_title
text: (Continued from Page 1.)

label: text
text: "The jurisdiction of this court," said Mr. Alabaster, "extends over acts committed within the 'territorial' waters of the Colony; secondly over persons on board" British ships in foreign waters in places where big ships go; thirdly over those waters generally known as the high seas which are under no territorial jurisdiction of any country but are free to the world.

label: text
text: "But it does not, however, extend to acts committed by foreigners in foreign waters or on foreign land. In fact, piracy on the high, sens which is justicable in every country is an entirely separate and distinct offence from piracy by municipal law of each different nation."

label: text
text: In support of his argument, Mr. Alabaster cited many legal cases, including the case of Kwok Ah-sing, a Chinese arrested in Hong Kong on a charge of murder and, piracy aboard a French vessel fifty miles from the coast of China. Whilst detained in Hong Kong for extradition, proceedings were taken under Habeus Corpus, as a result of which he was released. He was then re-arrested for piracy on the high seas and again released under Habeus Corpus on the grounds that he could not be indicted twice for the same offence.

label: text
text:
When the case was taken to the Privy Council, it was held that the Second release was wrong in that piracy on the high seas and piracy under municipal law were two separate and distinct crimes. Reading from the judgment Mr. Alabaster said that any nation might make its own laws for dealing with offences committed by its own subjects outside its own territory, but the general principle of criminal jurisprudence was that the quality of the acclone depended on the law of the place where it is committed.
The offence which these people have committed, assuming for the purposes of my argument that the Crown has proved its case, continued Mr. Alabaster, in an offence against the law of China for which the remedy of the Crown is to hold them pending an application from the Chinese authorities for their extradition. Under the present Ordinance, amended to more strongly emphasise the point subsequent to the Kwok An-sing case, Chinese subjects committing crimes within the jurisdiction of China have to be surrendered to the Chinese authorities even though the case might be a piracy "jurgentum" (by the law of the na

label: text
text: In Kwok Ah-sing's case it was stated, "further contended Mr. Alabaster, that piracy on the high seas was robbery within Admiralty jurisdiction" and in case it should be argued by the Crown that the Admiralty jurisdiction extended to rivers in foreign countries below the bridges where great ships go, he (Mr. Alabaster) must anticipate it by stating that this jurisdiction of the Admiralty was limited to British ships.

label: text
text: Mr. Alabaster cited cases on the point.

label: text
text: Mr. Dyer Ball, for the Crown, said that the defence had come as a great surprise to him. He submitted that the defence should have been made before the charge was put.

label: text
text: His Honour (Mr. Justice Wood) said that that could hardly be done until evidence had been called as to locality.

label: text
text: Eventually, His Honour adjourned the case until the afternoon for legal argument as to whether the onus was on the Crown or prisoners' counsel to prove whether the offence was committed within territorial waters.

label: paragraph_title
text: MINERS' VIEW OF NEW PROPOSALS:

label: text
text: REPLY TO MR. BALDWIN

label: text
text: The miners' executive yesterday and to-day discussed the letter from the Prime Minister to the Miners' secretary on September 18, in which Mr. Baldwin stated that the Mining Association declined to make a national agreement with the Miners' Federation but the Association declared that the 'con' owners in all districts were willing to observe the main principles which a national agreement would be designed to secure.

label: text
text: Mr. Baldwin's letter enclosed a memorandum explaining the National Arbitration Tribunal which the Government would establish—failing the conclusion of a national agreement—as soon as work was generally resumed. Though provisional settlements might be made locally the Tribunal might confirm or modify such settlements on appeal.

label: text
text: The Miners' Executive today replied that in the event of the stoppage being prolonged by an attempt to force back the miners on district agreements the responsibility would rest with the Government and the owners. The miners adhered to the principle of national negotiation and agreements. They desired an honourable settlement, but would not be coerced into accepting terms which they considered unjust. Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: No Change.

label: text
text: London. Sept. 21

label: text
text: A number of the Miners' Executive conferred with Mr. Baldwin this evening, for an hour and a half. They afterward declared that from the miners' viewpoint there had been "little or no change" in the position.

label: text
text: Messrs. Cook, Herbert Smith, and wo others remained behind to continue the discussion.—Reuter.

label: text
text: Nearly A Deadlock.

label: text
text: The coal conversations continued at Downing Street till one o'clock when it was officially announced that they are being resumed later to-day.

label: text
text: A flat rejection of the Government's proposals and the inevitable deadlock were narrowly averted during the two days' discussion of the proposals by the Miners' Executive. The leaders decided to ask Mr. Baldwin for an interview to explain what they regarded as a wide' divergence between Mr. Churchill's scheme—which the miners interpreted as confirmation by the Government of the principle of national negotiations and agreements—and Mr. Baldwin's proposals, which the miners contend are diametrically opposed to those of Mr. Churchill.

label: text
text: The miners are particularly suspicious of Mr. Baldwin's National Arbitration Tribunal. They suggest that if there must be one it should be established before the men resume work as a guarantee of good faith.—Reuter.

label: text
text:
Object of Parley.
Rudby. Sent. 27

label: text
text: After spending two days in considering the Government's proposals of September 17 for a settlement of the coal dispute, the Minions Executive this afternoon sent a reply to Mr. Baldwin.

label: text
text: The executive declare that the proposals, if carried out, would involve an entire surrender of the principle of national negotiations and agreements. They claim that Mr. Winston Churchill on September 8, whilst not excluding district discussions, affirmed the Government's adherence to the principle of national negotiations and agreements.

label: text
text: The executive, add:—"If a genuine and lasting peace is to be achieved it must rest on a frank recognition of the fact that, whatever may be the difference between the districts the miners of Great Britain form a single body with common interests, and that they are entitled to insist that those interested shall continue to be protected by their national organisation."

label: text
text: In one sentence of the letter the Executive point out that the Government has not yet specified the construction of the National Tribunal to which it proposes that district agreements shall be referred:

label: text
text: After the despatch of this letter to Mr. Baldwin it became known that the Miners' Executive—without awaiting a reply from the Prime Minister—had requested an interview with him, and that a meeting had been arranged for a late hour to-night.

label: text
text: It is understood that the object of the Executive is to get a further explanation of the Government's proposals. The Executive, wish, Inter alia, to know how the Government proposes to constitute the National Appeal Tribunal and whether, if the Tribunal were set up, this could be done simultaneously with the return of men to work instead of a prior resumption of work being a condition of its establishment. British Wireless Service.

label: paragraph_title
text:
WRECK OF A DUTCH
CANTEEN.

label: text
text: N.C.O. KILLED.

label: text
text:
The newspapers report that serious disorders have broken out among the troops at Assen who were undergoing their annual manoeuvres. It is believed that the disorders were prearranged, as ball cartridges were recently missing.
A long route march in the sweltering heat yesterday was apparently the climax to the situation. On their return to barracks the men smashed the windows and wrecked the canteen. An N.C.O. was killed by rifle bullet, and there were other minor casualties.
No arrests have been made, but the Twelfth Regiment has been confined to barracks and an official investigation is being made.—Ren

label: text
text: The Hague, Sept. 21

label: text
text: In the speech from the Throne at the opening of the States General, the Queen stated the situation of the country gave ground for gratitude in many respects. Although shadows were not lacking, the economic restoration was proceeding very gradually. The country's financial situation demanded constant chere as a reduction of the burdens imposed on the population. was an indispensable condition for a durable improvement of the economic situation. This could be only achieved by careful financial administration. The Queen expressed gratification that the League of Nations had gained importance by the entry of Germany.

label: text
text: Bills foreshadowed include a measure to provide that Dutchmen living outside the country should bear an equitable share of the Income and Capital Taxes and render their property liable to Succession Duty.

label: text
text:
It is also proposed to ratify certain draft conventions for the international organisation of labour.
The speech stated that the new Constitution for the Dutch East Indies would come completely into force next Spring. A policy aiming at prosperity for that colony would be energetically pursued and particularly in the interest of the native population.—Reuter.

label: paragraph_title
text: POOR DEBTORS!

label: paragraph_title
text: MELLON AS HARD AS NAILS.

label: text
text:
Mr. Mellon has informed President Coolidge, on his first visit after his return from Europe, that there was no reason for any change in the American policy of insistence in the collection of war debts. He assured him that the trade prospects of the world were bright and he believed the debt settlements would be no burden to the debtor nations. He felt that France would ratify the Debt Agreement.
Mr. Mellon agreed with President Coolidge that the question of reductions of taxation should await at least another year.—Reuter's American Service.
